The response is claimed before the first asynchronous delivery step, so a second submission cannot resolve the same question. It is routed through the normal follow-up path while the claimed response continues delivering its attachments. I kept the session identity check and retained a per-attempt validity token so cancellation, replacement questions, delivery failures, and retries remain safe: an old callback cannot become current again after a retry, and a failed attempt releases only its own claim.

🟡 **bug** (medium)

The `findLastIndex(..., m => m.say === "checkpoint_created")` lookup now runs inside the background promise (after `commit()` resolves) instead of while this call is still the newest checkpoint. Since commits are no longer awaited, two `saveCheckpoint()` calls can overlap — the agent routinely runs several tools back to back, and the comment you added notes a commit can take seconds on large shadow git repos. When the earlier commit resolves, this lookup finds the *newest* `checkpoint_created` message and writes its hash there, so the message that actually belongs to that commit stays without a `lastCheckpointHash`; if the commits resolve out of order, a message can even end up carrying a different checkpoint's hash. Both cases corrupt the per-message hash that 'Restore checkpoint' and `doesLatestTaskCompletionHaveNewChanges()` rely on.

**建议**: Resolve the target message synchronously instead of by re-searching later: right after `await this.say("checkpoint_created")` capture the message index/`ts` of the message you just created, and inside the `.then()` callback update exactly that captured message (re-validate it still exists). Alternatively serialize commits by chaining/storing the in-flight promise.

🟡 **bug** (medium)

Dropping `await this.checkpointTracker.commit()` means `saveCheckpoint()` can return before `lastCheckpointHash` has been written to the last `checkpoint_created` message. Your own NOTE states the attempt-completion flow needs that hash to be present: `ToolExecutor` calls `saveCheckpoint(true)` and is always followed by `addNewChangesFlagToLastCompletionResultMessage()` → `doesLatestTaskCompletionHaveNewChanges()`, which reads the latest checkpoint hash to decide whether to show the 'see new changes' button. With the commit now running in the background (and taking seconds on large repos), the hash is very likely still missing at that point, so the flag/button may silently stop appearing after `attempt_completion`.

**建议**: Keep a handle to the commit promise and await it when the caller needs the hash before continuing, e.g. capture `const commitPromise = this.checkpointTracker.commit().then(...)` and then `if (isAttemptCompletionMessage) { await commitPromise }` so the existing `saveCheckpoint(true)` contract is preserved while normal checkpoints stay non-blocking. If this is already handled elsewhere, a short comment stating where would help.

`request()` coalesces a newer request into `pending`, but it doesn't invalidate an already-active rebuild for the same reason — `cancellationGeneration` only moves in `cancel()` (line 40). So the active run's `isCurrent()` stays `true`, and once it finishes the newer request rebuilds the session again.

There's a correctness window here, not just redundant work. If the active rebuild has already snapshotted its config when the newer setting arrives, it installs the superseded one; and for checkpoint rebuilds it can replay a deferred follow-up from the shared `checkpointTransition` before the newer rebuild applies the latest setting — so a real message can run under the old checkpoint config.

I don't think bumping the generation here is a self-contained fix: the transition object is shared between the active and queued requests, and an invalidated rebuild returning from `replaceActiveSession()` can still clear `this.checkpointTransition` and stop the replacement. Either make a same-reason request explicitly supersede the active run with the transition ownership handled to match, or rename `isCurrent()` so it's clear it only means "not cancelled". A scheduler test for requesting a reason while that reason is actively rebuilding would pin whichever contract you pick.

Thanks — you were right on both counts, and the second one hid a real defect.

`isCurrent()` in a78223a means exactly "no newer request for the same reason has arrived": `request()` stamps a per-reason generation, and a running rebuild's context reads it live. `cancel()` and the per-reason cancellation generation are gone; nothing could reach them because `runTaskTransition` waits for the drain first.

The shared `checkpointTransition` is gone too. Holding a follow-up outside Core's queue meant nothing rendered it: a message typed during a turn after toggling Checkpoints vanished from the chat until the turn ended (this is what the e2e was failing on across all three CI platforms). Follow-ups now always go to Core's queue. The scheduler treats a session with queued prompts as busy, since Core drains the queue the instant a turn ends, and a send that settles after Core already started the next queued turn no longer flips the session idle. There is a scheduler test for a same-reason request during an active rebuild, and coordinator tests for supersession before replacement.

`waitUntilSettled` has no production caller left — this PR removes the one that existed (`await this.sessionRebuilds.waitUntilSettled()` in `SdkController`), and the send path now goes through `handlePendingRebuilds`, which parks the follow-up and returns `"deferred"` rather than awaiting. Only the scheduler's own tests reference it now. Worth dropping unless a caller is coming: a test-only affordance on a production class tends to acquire one later without the concurrency implications getting re-examined.

Dropped in b3cb45d, along with `hasPendingRebuild` and the settled-waiter list. The follow-up path no longer awaits the scheduler at all; a running-turn follow-up goes straight to Core's queue and the rebuild waits for the queue to drain.

Valid catch — a cancel landing while a retry's `doStream()` was pending saw no active reader, and the freshly resolved stream was then drained unattended. Fixed by checking for cancellation at the top of each attempt and cancelling the fresh provider stream instead of attaching a reader; this also covers a cancel arriving before the pump's first read. Added a regression test ("cancels a retry attempt whose doStream() resolves after the consumer cancelled") that fails against the previous revision.

Valid — fixed. Two notes for the record. First, this is pre-existing: `main`'s empty-response backoff sleeps with no signal at all and re-dials regardless; this PR made it visible by making the sibling network-retry path abort-aware. Second, the impact is smaller than a new provider generation starting: the re-dialed `doStream()` carries the request's already-aborted signal, so `fetch` rejects before opening a socket — the actual effect was the abort surfacing up to one backoff (250ms by default) late, via the re-dial's rejection rather than a clean check.

The empty path now sleeps on the merged abort/cancel signal and surfaces the abort before re-dialing, mirroring the network path — I kept the `controller.error(...)` + `return` idiom used there rather than the suggested `throw`, for consistency. Added a regression test ("stops retrying when the user aborts during the empty-response backoff sleep") that times out against the previous revision.

Fixed in `1544b995b`. The tool runner from `mcpRunner` in `runners.ts` now keeps the `connect()` promise. When that connect did not finish before the deadline, it disconnects again once the connect resolves, so a late connection is closed. The read still rejects at its deadline, and the connect attempt itself is not cancelled; `connectors.test.ts` covers this in "a connection that comes up after the read gave up on it is closed".

[P2] Clean up inherited pipes when the fallback settles. Resolving leaves stdout/stderr and their data listeners active. Reproduced: the hook returned after 1.02s, but Node stayed alive until its background child exited at 3.54s. A persistent child can keep the host alive and keep accumulating output. Add once-only pipe/listener and timer cleanup, with a test that checks host exit after settlement.

good catch, thanks!

The fallback now drops stdin/stdout/stderr (listeners included) right after it settles so the grandchild can't keep the host alive or keep filling the buffers. 

Added a test that counts the process's active pipe handles before and after — it fails on the old code (pipes stay until the grandchild exits) and passes now. Also, added a line to the hooks readme telling authors to give a backgrounded child its own stdio, since anything it writes to the inherited pipes after the hook exits is gone.

good call. I measured it in local runs..

An idle toggle flips in about 85ms, same as main. The switch only waits if you click it while a session is still being set up: right after another switch, right after sending a new task’s first message, or right after resuming a task from history. How long it waits is almost entirely the remote-config fetch every session start does:
- fast API: a rebuild takes about 300ms
- API delayed 1.5s: about 1.8s
- API unresponsive: the fetch waits out its 10s timeout, so a rebuild takes about 10.3s, and a toggle landing mid-rebuild sat unflipped for 6.3s in my run

I tried to play with other factors (repo size, a hundred rules, skills and workflows, long transcripts and MCP), and they barely moved it.

For comparison, those same three moments are exactly when main breaks. The switch flips instantly, but the session ends up in the other mode. A slow API makes that more likely in exactly the cases where this PR waits longer.

So **yes, the “stuck” switch is real on slow networks**. But I think the inconsistent state is the bigger problem. It’s silent, it doesn’t heal on its own (toggling back and forth didn’t help the reporter), and it costs the user real work. The stuck switch is visible, ends on its own, and is safe: clicking again just asks for the same mode, and anything sent meanwhile waits and runs in the mode you end up seeing.

For the toggle itself, we could do this as a follow-up:
1. Flip the switch immediately with a pending state (dimmed slider or a “Switching to Act…” tooltip), and flip it back with a short explanation if the switch fails. Maybe a notification only if the wait gets long, so it doesn’t nag on every slow toggle
2. Coalesce rapid toggles, so Plan then Act before the first rebuild starts only rebuilds once

Intentional, keeping this. #14971 removed the deadline on purpose: the server can commit the switch after the client gives up, and only its answer triggers the auth refresh that moves this window onto the new account. With a client deadline, the UI stayed on the old account while billing used the new one. `main` has never had a deadline on this PUT either. The UI wait is still capped at 10 seconds by `setUserOrganization`. The only new effect is that a later switch queues behind one the server never answers, which takes a server or proxy that hangs without failing. We'll revisit if that shows up in practice.
